author: Claude (English teacher role), v2 after expert audit
basis: Rewritten against the v2 quality gate after two independent expert audits (CEFR assessor; speech coach + fact checker) found the v1 text passed on averages while individual slides missed their band, A2 and B1 were the same sentences with synonyms swapped, and several facts had drifted. Facts corrected to source: +1.6 degrees over a century (NSTC 2024) against a global 1.3; Climate Change Response Act 2023; carbon fee live 2025; Taichung capture demonstration about 2,000 t/yr, not a deployed solution; public transport share is about 14%, so 'we rely on public transport' was removed; 'Silicon Shield' dropped as a cross-strait deterrence term unsuited to a climate talk. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count.

slides.1: Something has shifted in the way our seasons behave, and the record heat, sudden flooding and vanishing winters are no longer unusual events. They are the local signature of a global emergency.
slides.2: The thirteenth global goal asks every government to cut emissions and to build real defences against disaster. Taiwan, although shut out of the main climate negotiations, has chosen to meet the identical standard.
slides.3: Geography leaves us very little margin. We are a crowded island on the typhoon track, with a low western coastline and an export-driven economy built around power-hungry manufacturing that never stops.
slides.4: Consider the measurements rather than the impressions. A century of observations shows Taiwan warming by 1.6 degrees against a global 1.3, positioning our island among the faster-warming regions of the planet.
slides.5: What holds us back is structural, not moral. Coal and imported gas still dominate electricity generation, and the chip industry that underwrites our prosperity cannot lose even a single hour of supply.
slides.6: Two uncomfortable questions follow from that. If industrial demand keeps climbing, can clean power ever really overtake it, and if it cannot, which generation absorbs the debt we are quietly building?
slides.7: Progress has nonetheless been substantial. The 2023 Act wrote net zero by 2050 into statute, and a carbon fee introduced in 2025 now bills the largest emitters for what they release.
slides.8: Two industries now mark our shoreline. Offshore turbines face the Strait in their hundreds, while solar installations have taken over campus roofs, fish farms and industrial parks the length of the island.
slides.9: Public effort here is genuine but not enough. Recycling rates beat those of most economies, yet petrol scooters still rule everyday travel, so personal habit cannot substitute for structural reform.
slides.10: Engineers are rebuilding the grid around software rather than switchgear. The intention is that a program allocates power minute by minute, and Taipower has moved from modelling into limited trials.
slides.11: Carbon capture illustrates both the promise and the scale of this work. A demonstration unit at Taichung removes roughly 2,000 tonnes annually, which proves the underlying science while remaining negligible beside the plant's total output.
slides.12: Urban travel offers a more convincing example. Electric scooters manufactured here operate on a battery exchanged in seconds, and thousands of swap points now form a refuelling network of national scale.
slides.13: Cutting carbon nevertheless imposes real costs on the smallest firms. Cleaner equipment needs money that small factories seldom hold, so a transition designed without support will simply move the hardship elsewhere.
slides.14: Energy security remains politically unresolved. Only when storage improves will that choice get easier, because precision factories demand power every hour while wind and solar output keeps rising and falling.
slides.15: Carbon does not stop at a border. Taiwan holds technology worth sharing, yet exclusion from the international climate negotiations limits how far that knowledge can in practice travel beyond our shores.
slides.16: Staying sceptical is part of being a citizen. Companies now market their green virtue while altering very little, so insist on audited figures and dated promises rather than photographs of turbines.
slides.17: The direction is encouraging without yet being sufficient. The law exists, offshore capacity is expanding and the first capture trials have begun, yet renewable generation still sits below our own target.
slides.18: It is your cohort, not mine, that will supply the engineers, voters and consumers of the coming decades. Those decisions, once taken, will simply outlive every administration currently holding office.
slides.19: Giving up solves nothing, whereas curiosity actually gets somewhere. So interrogate the science, verify the figures you are given, and share whatever you find out as clearly as you can.
slides.20: That brings the question back to this room: will your generation merely inherit this transition, or will you actually engineer it? Taiwan is ready to deliver on SDG 13, and I have personally decided that I am.
